courses.title: Peace and Conflict Resolution (GST 312)
courses.description: General-studies course on the nature of peace and conflict, causes of conflict in Nigeria, conflict resolution methods, and peace-building — including conflict in the health workplace.

topics.title: Concepts of Peace and Conflict
topics.summary: Definitions, types of peace and conflict, and theories of conflict.

material.heading: Peace
material.body: Johan Galtung, regarded as the father of peace studies, distinguished negative peace (the absence of direct violence or war) from positive peace (the presence of social justice, equity and conditions that prevent violence). He also described direct violence (physical harm), structural violence (harm built into unjust social structures — e.g. poverty, unequal access to health care) and cultural violence (beliefs that justify violence).

material.heading: Conflict and theories
material.body: Conflict is a struggle between parties who perceive incompatible goals, scarce resources or interference. It is natural and can be constructive (driving change) or destructive. Levels: intrapersonal, interpersonal, intragroup, intergroup, and international. Theories: structural conflict theory (inequalities in society — Marx), relative deprivation / frustration–aggression theory (the gap between expectations and reality leads to aggression — Ted Gurr), human needs theory (unmet basic needs — Burton), and psychocultural theory (identity and fear).
keyPoints: Conflict can be constructive or destructive

topics.title: Causes and Types of Conflict in Nigeria
topics.summary: Ethnic, religious, resource, political and communal conflicts in Nigeria.

material.heading: Causes
material.body: Common causes of conflict in Nigeria include competition over land and resources (farmer–herder conflicts in the Middle Belt), ethno-religious tensions (e.g. crises in Jos, Kaduna), political competition and electoral violence, chieftaincy and boundary disputes (e.g. Ife–Modakeke, Aguleri–Umuleri), resource control and environmental degradation in the Niger Delta, youth unemployment, poverty, and insurgency and terrorism (Boko Haram in the North-East since about 2009), as well as banditry and kidnapping.
keyPoints: Farmer–herder conflicts over land and water
Boko Haram insurgency in the North-East

material.heading: Effects on health
material.body: Conflict kills and injures, displaces people into internally displaced persons (IDP) camps, destroys health facilities, disrupts immunisation (e.g. hampering polio eradication), increases malnutrition, sexual and gender-based violence and mental health problems such as post-traumatic stress disorder, and drives health workers away. Humanitarian law protects health workers and facilities during armed conflict; the Red Cross emblem signals protection.

topics.title: Conflict Management and Resolution Methods
topics.summary: Negotiation, mediation, arbitration, adjudication and alternative dispute resolution.

material.heading: Styles of handling conflict
material.body: The Thomas–Kilmann model describes five styles based on assertiveness and cooperativeness: competing (win–lose), accommodating (lose–win), avoiding (lose–lose), compromising (partial win–partial win) and collaborating (win–win, problem-solving). Collaboration is best for important long-term relationships; avoidance may suit trivial issues.
keyPoints: Thomas–Kilmann: compete, accommodate, avoid, compromise, collaborate

material.heading: Methods
material.body: Negotiation is direct discussion between parties to reach agreement. Mediation involves a neutral third party who facilitates communication but does not impose a decision. Conciliation is similar, with the third party suggesting terms. Arbitration involves a neutral arbitrator whose decision is usually binding. Adjudication (litigation) is resolution by the courts. Alternative dispute resolution (ADR) refers to methods outside court — negotiation, mediation, conciliation, arbitration — which are quicker and cheaper and preserve relationships. Traditional African methods use elders, chiefs, age grades and religious leaders. Early warning and early response systems detect rising tensions.
keyPoints: Mediation: third party facilitates, no imposed decision

topics.title: Peace-building, Human Rights and Security
topics.summary: Peacekeeping versus peace-building, human rights, and institutions for peace.

material.heading: Peace processes
material.body: Peacemaking brings parties to agreement (diplomacy, negotiation); peacekeeping maintains a ceasefire, often with neutral forces such as UN or ECOMOG troops (Nigeria led ECOMOG in Liberia and Sierra Leone in the 1990s); peace-building addresses root causes to prevent relapse — reconciliation, disarmament, demobilisation and reintegration (DDR), rebuilding institutions, justice and development. The Niger Delta Amnesty Programme (2009) offered DDR to militants. Transitional justice includes truth commissions (e.g. the Oputa Panel in Nigeria, 1999–2002).

material.heading: Human rights and institutions
material.body: Human rights are inherent entitlements of every person, set out in the Universal Declaration of Human Rights (1948) and, for Africa, the African Charter on Human and Peoples' Rights (1981). Chapter IV of the 1999 Nigerian Constitution guarantees fundamental rights (life, dignity, personal liberty, fair hearing, privacy, freedom of thought and religion, expression, movement, and freedom from discrimination). The National Human Rights Commission promotes and protects them. International organisations for peace include the United Nations (1945), African Union (2002, successor to the OAU founded 1963) and ECOWAS (1975).
keyPoints: Chapter IV of the 1999 Constitution: fundamental rights

topics.title: Conflict in the Health-care Workplace
topics.summary: Sources of conflict among health workers and patients, strikes, and constructive handling.

material.heading: Sources
material.body: Health-care workplaces are prone to conflict because of heavy workloads, staff shortages, hierarchy and role ambiguity between professions (inter-professional rivalry), scarce resources, poor communication, remuneration disputes and industrial action (strikes by health unions), and patients' or relatives' frustration over delays, costs or poor outcomes, which may lead to aggression against staff. Poorly handled conflict harms teamwork and patient safety.

material.heading: Constructive handling
material.body: Constructive approaches include clear communication (active listening, 'I' statements), clarifying roles and shared goals centred on patients, structured tools (SBAR), timely feedback, fair grievance procedures, team meetings, mediation by supervisors or human resources, collective bargaining and social dialogue between unions and management, and de-escalation techniques with angry patients (stay calm, listen, acknowledge feelings, explain, set boundaries, and ensure safety). Workplace violence should be reported.

questions.explanation: Unclear roles and status competition fuel conflict.

questions.explanation: Calm listening de-escalates tension.
